generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, active engagement is the difference between a student who accepts a confident claim and one who asks what evidence it rests on. A coaching manual that says a drill develops agility, or a report that says a programme works, invites an active reader to ask how it was tested, in whom, and against what comparison. Opening up that question, rather than taking the claim as final, is the everyday habit across sport science, coaching and sport management alike.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two School of Sport students on a coaching module review the same training session plan.

Tom reads it, sees that it looks well organised, and writes that the plan is effective. The point is captured, but Tom has taken the plan at face value, with no sense of the evidence behind its drills or whether coaches would question it. This is passive engagement.

Amara pauses on the claim that the plan is effective. Effective for whom, and how would we know? She checks what the drills are meant to develop, compares them against training principles, and finds one drill with little evidence behind it. The plan goes into her notes as something to weigh, not a model to copy. This is active engagement: she has opened up the question.

Both read the same plan. Only Amara treated it as something to question.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, being critical becomes real work when you engage with a source actively: questioning its claim, checking the evidence, and bringing in other studies rather than accepting a single summary. You can now tell active engagement from passive and choose an active move when a claim sounds settled. The next lesson gives you the language to describe these moves.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that opened up the question around the source?

items.text: She checked what the drills develop, compared them against training principles, and found one with little evidence.
She accepted the plan because it looked well organised.
She read the plan more slowly than Tom did.
She copied the plan into her notes as a model to follow.

feedback.correct: That's right. Testing the plan against training principles and other evidence turned a confident claim into something to weigh.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that brought in other evidence or principles, rather than accepting or copying the plan.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara opened up the question by checking the drills against training principles and finding weak evidence. Accepting, re-reading or copying all leave the plan as the last word.
